Bike has been recovered. I went through a huge process to get it. At first they tried to send me away.  I told them my wife had spoken to 3 people, and they had told her we could just come and get it. Then I had to wait to a security guy to drive me to the secret storage places. I looked at about 200 bikes. The security guy said I could take one of those but they were all kind of crappy. Then he said there is one more place where they store the more expensive bikes. He drove me back to where we started. He got the keys from another security guard and opened a steel door to a concrete room with a low ceiling inside a parking structure. I looked at another 6 rows of bikes, maybe another 100 bikes. Then I finally found it with the only 3 more to go. He told me during our drive about being a USC safety officer. They are actually sworn police and part of the LAPD. But they are not called police yet because the old administration did not want them to be too threatening. But the new administration is pro police. He said that some of the USC kids are gang members. Sometimes the gang pays for their education. Vietnamese gangs and MS13. Someone explain to me why is the drywall sandwiched like this?  If the drywall was attached to the soffit and finish textured and painted,  and then the 2X12 was added a few years later, that wouldn't make sense because the soffit without the 2 X 12 would be very weak and most likely would visibly sag. So I don't think the 2 X 12 was added as part of a remodelling, I think the 2 X 12 was there from the very beginning,  or at least the same time the soffit was installed.  The soffit is necessary for hiding the HVAC ducting and it matches the positioning of the fire sprinklers too, so I think the soffit is most likely original construction and if it's not,  there was some other framing there before. Also note the 2X4 blocking of the soffit would be so weak it would be a joke without the 2X12. So if the 2 X 12 was there from the beginning why did they use the 2 X 4 blocking at all?  And why would they sandwich drywall in between  framing members? It doesn't make any sense to me.  I could understand if it was framed 1st with 2X4 to line everything up and then the stronger straighter non sagging 2X12 was added, perhaps that would be a way of using more wood but making it easier to line everything up and do it step-by-step. But that wouldn't explain why the drywall was sandwiched in between.

Don't leave money on the table. If you have plaster walls chances are your wall height is 8' 3". That extra 3" may not seem like a lot, but you can do the math in your head. 8' Ã 12" is 96". So a regular 8' wall is pretty close to 100". So that extra 3" is roughly 3%. Actually a tiny bit more than 3%. So let's say you have $10,000 worth of wall painting. 3% of that equals $300, before O&P and sales tax. So who is telling me that the price for an estimator should be a $350 flat fee? The 3" difference is almost equal to the low price estimator fee on just one measurement error on one line item.  Also, getting your measurements and your sketch correct gives a lot of credibility to the estimate. You can go round and round with subjective arguments all day long about whether something is high grade or low grade. But when you're negotiating with the insurance company or going to appraisal  and you can say that your measurements are accurate and the other person's measurements are not, that's not a subjective difference.

Best way to attach a sole plate or so plate to the slab on a new pour is to use a j-bolt. On a retrofit the best way is to drill a hole and epoxy a bolt. In California the contractor will be babysat by a deputy inspector who watches the process and signs off on it. Because of earthquakes. The next best method is to use a redhead, one of these expansion bolts, they're supposed to go in 7 in but a lot of people use the shorter ones and as long as the building inspector doesn't see the Box they might get away with it because you can't tell from looking once it's installed. But you shouldn't do that and it's probably not code compliant as far as I know in California but it's okay in other states to use those expansion bolts. One brand name is redhead and people often refer to him by the brand name. The least effective method is the one I'm doing here just to hold my soleplate temporarily, it's a powder actuated nail gun that drives a nail into the concrete. It uses a little 22 caliber blank and you can choose from different loads. All of these things are in Xactimate.

Can we really trust our common sense to determine what evidence means? If you see some green mold is that conclusive evidence that the leak must be 2 months old? A lot of times we use our interpretation of Visual Evidence to decide that something happened a long time ago or happened recently but are we making wrong assumptions sometimes? On both sides of the fence in claims. Check out this very delicate spider web that survived historically heavy Southern California rain driving at 30 miles an hour. Anybody seeing this spiderweb the day after the rain would naturally assume it had been freshly made that morning or the night before. I never would have imagined a delicate spider web would survive even just one day of heavy rain. Or a 10 minute drive at 30 mph.

A common Xactimate question is how do I add stairs after I drew the room? I've been saying this forever. See this scene in a detective movie. They 1) revisit the crime scene, presumably to examine PHYSICAL EVIDENCE and 2) "chat up the neighbors", presumably to gather HUMAN INTELLIGENCE AKA EYEWITNESS TESTIMONY.

This is routine in investigations.

Unless it's an engineer doing an "investigation" for an insurance carrier. They do #1 but never #2.

They never ask anyone who witnessed the hail or the wind. They never ask the homeowner when repairs were done, before or after the wind event. They never ask when the shingles were last installed. They never ask about things that would corroborate the wind event like trash cans blowing down the street, trees falling over, and they don't ask about things that would corroborate hail like damaged vehicles. They just don't ever ask.

Why do detectives and police officers always do #1 and #2 but engineers only do #1?
